lists.title: Xhosa A1 Grammar
lists.description: Foundations: subject concords, the first noun classes, copulatives, negation, locatives, having.

lists.title: Xhosa A2 Grammar
lists.description: Possessive/object/adjective concords, recent past, future, demonstratives.

lists.title: Xhosa B1 Grammar
lists.description: Negation across tenses, subjunctive, remote past, relative clauses.

lists.title: Xhosa C2 Grammar
lists.description: Mastery: amaqhalo, hlonipha, and the particles and greetings of real conversation.

points.title: Subject concords and the present (ndi-, u-, ba-…)
points.explanation:
Every verb starts with a subject concord: ndi- (I), u- (you / he-she cl.1), si- (we), ni- (you all), ba- (they).

The long present adds -ya- when nothing follows the verb: Ndiyafunda (I am studying); with an object the -ya- drops: Ndifunda isiXhosa (I study Xhosa).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.hint: to learn + 'I' concord (no -ya- before an object)

points.title: Noun classes 1/2: um-/aba- (people)
points.function: Talk about people, one or many
points.explanation:
Xhosa nouns carry class prefixes.

Class 1/2 is the people class: umntu/abantu (person/people), umfundi/abafundi (student/students), umntwana/abantwana (child/children), umfazi/abafazi (woman/women).

Names, kinship terms and titles sit in class 1a instead — u- in the singular, oo- in the plural: utitshala/ootitshala (teacher/teachers). They still take class 1 and class 2 agreement: utitshala omnye, ootitshala ababini.

The class drives agreement on everything that follows.
points.culture_note: The class system (about 15 classes) is the engine of the whole language — one class pair at a time is the way in.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.hint: class 1a takes oo- in the plural

points.title: Noun classes 5/6 and 7/8
points.function: Use the ili-/ama- and isi-/izi- families
points.explanation:
Xhosa's class prefixes come in singular/plural pairs:

| Class | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5/6 | `i(li)-` | `ama-` |
| 7/8 | `isi-` | `izi-` |

Class 5/6: ilizwe/amazwe (country/countries), iqanda/amaqanda (egg/eggs), ihashe/amahashe (horse/horses). Class 7/8: isitya/izitya (dish/dishes). `isi-` also names languages: isiXhosa, isiNgesi (English).

Class 5 agreement is `li-`: Ilizwe likhulu (the country is big).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Noun classes 9/10: in-/izin-
points.explanation:
Class 9/10 covers many everyday nouns and animals: inja/izinja (dog/dogs), indlu/izindlu (house/houses), incwadi/iincwadi (book/books), imoto/iimoto (car/cars).

The plural has two shapes, and the stem decides which. A one-syllable stem keeps izin-: inja → izinja, indlu → izindlu. A longer stem lengthens the i- instead: incwadi → iincwadi, imoto → iimoto.

Their agreements use i-/zi-: Inja iyatya (The dog is eating), Izinja ziyatya (The dogs are eating).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Identifying copulatives (ngu-, yi-)
points.explanation:
'It is X' is a prefix on the noun, and which prefix depends on the noun's class:

| Class | Prefix | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `ngu-` | ngumfundi |
| 1a | `ngu-` | nguThemba |
| 5 | `li-` | liqanda |
| 7 | `si-` | sisitya |
| 9 | `yi-` | yincwadi |

So nguThemba (this is Themba), yincwadi (this is a book).

The negative is `asi-`, with o in place of the prefix's vowel, and the noun loses its own initial vowel: umfundi → asingomfundi (he is not a student).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Present negative (andi-…-i)
points.explanation:
Wrap the verb in a negative concord and change the final -a to -i: ndiyafunda → andifundi (I don't study), uyafuna → akafuni (he doesn't want), bayasebenza → abasebenzi (they don't work).

The concord changes shape as well: ndi- becomes andi-, u- becomes aka-, ba- becomes aba-. The -ya- of the long present has no place in the negative.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.hint: to speak + negative, I (final vowel changes)

drills.translation: I don't live in Cape Town.

points.title: Locatives (e-…-ini)
points.explanation:
Places are made with e-, and most nouns take an ending on the back as well: isikolo → esikolweni (at school), indlu → endlwini (in the house), idolophu → edolophini (in town).

The ending's vowel copies the noun's last vowel: -ini after i and u, -eni after a, e and o.

Place names take e- on its own: iKapa → eKapa (in Cape Town), iGoli → eGoli (in Johannesburg). A few ordinary nouns do too: ifama → efama (on the farm).

Ndihlala eKapa (I live in Cape Town), Ndiya esikolweni (I'm going to school).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I am going to town tomorrow.
The children play in the park.

points.title: Questions (ntoni, bani, phi)
points.explanation:
Question words follow the verb: Ufuna ntoni? (What do you want?), Ngubani igama lakho? (What/who is your name?), Uhlala phi? (Where do you live?).

Yes/no questions just use rising intonation, or open with Ingaba: Ingaba uyeza? (Are you coming?).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.hint: interrogative probing the time of the action — not its place or agent
interrogative probing the place of the action — not its time or manner

points.title: To have: -na-
points.explanation:
'Have' fuses -na- with the noun: ndi + na + incwadi → Ndinencwadi (I have a book), Unemali (you have / she has money), Banabantwana (they have children).

Negative: Andinamali (I have no money).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Possessive concords (yam, wam, bam…)
points.explanation:
The possessive agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner:

| Class | Concord | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `wa-` | umntwana wam |
| 2 | `ba-` | abantwana bam |
| 5 | `la-` | igama lam |
| 7 | `sa-` | isitya sam |
| 9 | `ya-` | incwadi yam |

The owner is the ending: `-m` (my), `-kho` (your), `-khe` (his, her), `-bo` (their) — incwadi yam, incwadi yakho, incwadi yakhe, incwadi yabo.

Our and your (plural) are the exception: they put e in place of the concord's a — incwadi yethu, incwadi yenu.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Recent past (-ile)
points.explanation:
The recent past ends in -ile when the verb closes the clause: Ndifundile (I studied / have studied), Bafikile (They have arrived). Before an object the short form -e is used: Ndibone umfundi?

— commonly Ndibonile in isolation; keep -ile clause-final at this level.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Future (-za ku-)
points.explanation:
The future combines -za (come) with the infinitive ku-: Ndiza kufunda (I will study), Uza kufika ngomso (she will arrive tomorrow), Siza kuthetha (we will talk).

Before a vowel-initial stem ku- becomes kw-: Uza kwenza ntoni ngomso? (What are you going to do tomorrow?). A consonant-initial stem keeps it: Siza kuya eKapa (we are going to go to Cape Town).

In speech it contracts to -zo- (ndizofunda), and ndiza ku- is often written solid as ndizakufunda.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I am going to work tomorrow.
We are going to go to Cape Town.
drills.hint: infinitive 'to go' after the future marker

drills.translation: The children are going to play.
What are you going to do tomorrow?

points.title: Object concords
points.function: Point the verb at its object
points.explanation:
The object can live inside the verb, as a concord between the subject concord and the stem:

| Class | Object concord | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `-m-` | Ndiyambona |
| 2 | `-ba-` | Ndiyabathanda |
| 6 | `-wa-` | Ndiyawasela |
| 7 | `-si-` | Ndiyasithetha |
| 9 | `-yi-` | Ndiyayifunda |
| 10 | `-zi-` | Ndiyazithanda |

The noun itself is then left out, or set off ahead of the verb: Incwadi? Ndiyayifunda (The book? I am reading it).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: The book? I am reading it.
The water? I am drinking it.

points.title: Adjective concords (omhle, entle…)
points.explanation:
An adjective takes a concord from its noun's class:

| Class | Concord | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `om-` | umntwana omhle |
| 2 | `aba-` | abantwana abahle |
| 5 | `eli-` | iqanda elikhulu |
| 7 | `esi-` | isitya esihle |
| 9 | `en-` | incwadi entle |
| 10 | `ezin-` | izindlu ezinkulu |

The stem stays the same — `-hle` (beautiful), `-khulu` (big), `-ncinci` (small) — except after the class 9/10 nasal, which hardens it: `-hle` becomes `-ntle` (incwadi entle), `-khulu` becomes `-nkulu` (indlu enkulu, izindlu ezinkulu).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Demonstratives (lo, le, eli…)
points.explanation:
Demonstratives agree with the class: lo mntu (this person, cl.1), le ncwadi (this book, cl.9), eli qanda (this egg, cl.5), esi sitya (this dish, cl.7), aba bantwana (these children, cl.2).

'That' lengthens: loo, leyo, elo…

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Negative past and future
points.explanation:
The negative past wraps the verb in a-…-anga: Andifundanga (I didn't study), Andithenganga (I didn't buy), Abafikanga (they didn't arrive).

That a- fuses with the subject concord, exactly as in the present negative: ndi- → andi-, u- (class 1) → aka-, ba- → aba-.

The negative future puts the same a- on the auxiliary -za, whose final vowel goes to -i: andizi kufunda (I will not study), akazi kufika (she won't arrive). The infinitive after it drops its initial u-: ukudlala → kudlala.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: Themba is not going to arrive tomorrow.
drills.hint: future negative, he — the short -zi form

drills.translation: We are not going to play tomorrow.
drills.hint: infinitive 'to play' after the negative future

points.title: Subjunctive (-e) and ma- (let's)
points.explanation:
The subjunctive swaps the final -a for **-e**, and it turns up in three places:

- ma- + concord, for a proposal: Masifunde! (Let's study!, ma- + si- + funda + -e)
- after ukuba, with a verb of wanting: Ndifuna ukuba ufunde (I want you to study)
- after ukuze, for purpose: Yiza ukuze sithethe (Come so that we talk)

Before a vowel-initial stem the concord loses its own vowel: ndi- + enza + -e → ndenze (that I do).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I want you to speak well.
What do you want me to do?

points.title: Remote past (a-…-a)
points.explanation:
The remote past fuses **-a-** into the subject concord: Ndahlala eKapa (I lived in Cape Town, back then), Wafunda eRhini (He studied in Makhanda), Sahlala eMonti (We lived in East London).

| Person | Concord | Remote past |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | ndi- | nda- |
| you (sg.), he/she | u- | wa- |
| we | si- | sa- |
| you (pl.) | ni- | na- |
| they | ba- | ba- |

Only ba- comes out unchanged, so bathetha is both 'they spoke, long ago' and the short present 'they speak'; the context separates them. It is the storytelling past.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I lived in Cape Town long ago.
I worked in Johannesburg long ago.
Mum lived in East London long ago.
We studied in Makhanda long ago.

points.title: Relative clauses (o-…-yo)
points.explanation:
A relative verb takes a relative concord and ends in **-yo**: umntwana ofundayo (the child who studies), abantwana abafundayo (the children who study), imoto ebalekayo (a car that goes fast).

The relative concord is a- plus the subject concord, with the vowels running together (a + i → e, a + u → o):

| Class | Subject | Relative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | u- | o- |
| 2 | ba- | aba- |
| 9 | i- | e- |
| 10 | zi- | ezi- |

A person concord works the same way (ndi- → endi-), and an object concord sits inside the verb: incwadi endiyifundayo (the book that I am reading, cl.9 -yi-).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: the book that I am reading

drills.hint: to love + relative frame with 'I' and a class-15 object

points.title: Passive (-wa)
points.function: Say what is done, without the doer
points.explanation:
The passive inserts -w- before the final vowel: funda → fundwa, thetha → thethwa, cula → culwa. The verb then agrees with its new subject: Incwadi iyafundwa (The book is being read), IsiXhosa sithethwa eKapa (Xhosa is spoken in Cape Town).

The perfect ends in -iwe instead: thatha → thathiwe (Imali ithathiwe, the money has been taken), enza → enziwe (Umsebenzi wenziwe, the work has been done).

Where the doer is named, ngu- marks it: Abantwana bathandwa ngumama (The children are loved by their mother).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: Xhosa is spoken in Cape Town.
The children are loved by their mother.

points.title: Causative (-isa)
points.explanation: -isa turns 'do' into 'cause to do': funda (learn) → fundisa (teach), sebenza (work) → sebenzisa (use — 'make work'): Utitshala ufundisa abantwana (The teacher teaches the children), Ndisebenzisa ifowuni (I use a phone).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: Mum is putting the child to sleep.
I am showing the book to the students.
The teachers teach the children Xhosa.

points.title: Applicative (-ela)
points.function: Do something for or to someone
points.explanation:
-ela replaces the final -a and adds a person or a direction to the action: bhala (write) → bhalela (write to/for), pheka (cook) → phekela (cook for), thenga (buy) → thengela (buy for), sebenza (work) → sebenzela (work for), hamba (go) → hambela (go to, visit).

The one the action is done for becomes the object, straight after the verb: Ndibhalela umama ileta (I am writing mother a letter), Usebenzela inkampani (She works for a company).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I am writing a letter to mother.
She works for a big company.
Mum cooks food for the children.
I am buying a book for my friend.
He sends money to his mother.
We are singing a song for the baby.

points.title: Reciprocal (-ana)
points.function: Say people do things to each other
points.explanation:
-ana replaces the final -a and makes the action mutual: thanda (love) → thandana (love each other), bona (see) → bonana (see each other), nceda (help) → ncedana (help each other), bulisa (greet) → bulisana (greet each other).

The subject has to be more than one: Bayathandana (They love each other), Sobonana ngomso (We'll see each other tomorrow), Oomama badibana edolophini (The mothers meet in town). With a single subject the other party comes in on na-: Ndidibana naye (I meet him).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: See you tomorrow! (we shall see each other)
People greet each other in the morning.

points.title: Conditions with ukuba
points.explanation:
**Ukuba** does three jobs, and English uses a different word for each:

- 'if', opening a condition: Ukuba uyafunda, uza kuphumelela (If you study, you will pass)
- 'that', after a verb of knowing or feeling: Ndiyazi ukuba uyeza (I know that you are coming)
- 'whether', after a verb of not knowing: Andazi ukuba uyeza (I don't know whether he is coming)

What ukuba never means is 'when'. That is xa with the participial: xa ndifunda (when I study), xa efika (when he arrives).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: If you study, you will pass.
I know that you are coming.
If you want to succeed, study.
drills.hint: the conjunction opening the condition on which the main clause depends

drills.translation: I don't know when he is going to arrive.
If it rains, we will stay in the house.
drills.hint: the conjunction that opens a conditional clause

drills.translation: I am glad that you have arrived.
drills.hint: complementiser after a verb of emotion, opening the clause reporting the news

points.title: Noun classes 11, 14, 15 (ulu-, ubu-, uku-)
points.explanation:
Each of these three classes has one prefix and one concord:

| Class | Prefix | Concord |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 11 | u(lu)- | lu- |
| 14 | ubu- | bu- |
| 15 | uku- | ku- |

Class 11 covers long or thin things and some mass nouns: ulwimi (language), uluvo (opinion), ubisi (milk). The prefix shows in full in some of them and reduces to u- in others, but the concord is lu- either way: Uluvo lwakho lubalulekile (Your opinion is important). The plural is class 10: ulwimi → iilwimi.

Class 14 carries abstracts (ubomi life, ubuhle beauty, ubuntu) and class 15 is the infinitive used as a noun (ukutya food/eating, ukufunda studying). Both stay singular.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: We love the beauty of this country.

points.title: Absolute pronouns (mna, wena, yena…)
points.explanation:
The concords already carry the grammar, so an absolute pronoun is there for emphasis or contrast: Mna ndiyasebenza namhlanje (As for me, I am working today).

| Person | Pronoun | with na- |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | mna | nam |
| you (sg.) | wena | nawe |
| he/she | yena | naye |
| we | thina | nathi |
| you (pl.) | nina | nani |
| they | bona | nabo |

The na- column is 'with' and also 'and': Ndiza kuhamba nawe (I will go with you). Nouns have absolute pronouns of their own, built on the class concord: yona (cl.9), lona (cl.5), sona (cl.7), zona (cl.10).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: As for ME, I am working today.
And YOU, what do you like?
As for ME, I like coffee.
And YOU, where do you live?

points.title: Persistive -sa- (still / no longer)
points.function: Say what's still going on — and what stopped
points.explanation:
-sa- sits between the subject concord and the stem and means 'still': ndisafunda (I am still studying), basadlala (they are still playing), usalele (she is still asleep, on the perfect lele).

In the negative it means 'no longer', and the present negative's own shape applies — a- on the concord and the final -a going to -i: andisahlali apha (I no longer live here), akasaseli (he no longer drinks).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: The children are still playing outside.
Do you still live in Cape Town?

drills.hint: to live + negative still = no longer (I)
to drink + negative still = no longer (he)

points.title: Counting with concords (ezimbini, bangaphi)
points.function: Count things — and make the number agree
points.explanation:
Number stems take the concord of the noun they count, so the numeral agrees with what is being counted:

| stem | number |
| --- | --- |
| -nye | one |
| -bini | two |
| -thathu | three |
| -ne | four |
| -hlanu | five |

- class 2: abantu ababini (two people)
- class 4: iminyaka emihlanu (five years)
- class 10: iincwadi ezimbini (two books)

The class-10 concord is the one shape you have to compute: it is ezin-, which shows its nasal as m before b and drops it before n — ezimbini, ezintathu, ezine.

-ngaphi asks how many with the same agreement: bangaphi abantu?

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

points.title: Instrumental nga- (ngemoto, ngesiXhosa)
points.function: Say by, with, in, and on-a-day with one prefix
points.explanation:
**Nga-** makes a by/with/in phrase, and its vowel fuses with the noun's own: an i- noun gives nge- (imoto → ngemoto, isandla → ngesandla), a u- noun gives ngo- (uvuyo → ngovuyo, uloliwe → ngololiwe).

One prefix covers several jobs:

- means: ngemoto (by car), ngololiwe (by train)
- instrument: ngesandla (by hand)
- medium: ngesiXhosa (in Xhosa)
- manner: ngovuyo (with joy)
- a day: ngoMvulo (on Monday)

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: They go to work by train.

points.title: When-clauses: xa + participial
points.explanation: Xa opens a when/while-clause and the verb goes participial — no -ya-, and class 1 subjects shift u- → e-, class 2 ba- → be-: xa ndifunda (when I study), xa utitshala ethetha (when the teacher speaks), xa abantwana bedlala (when the children are playing).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: When I study, I listen to music.
When it rains, we stay in the house.
I will be glad when you arrive.
When we have time, we eat together.
He listens when the teacher speaks.
drills.hint: to speak — participial class 1 (u- becomes e-)

drills.translation: When the children are playing, we are happy.
drills.hint: to play — participial class 2 (ba- becomes be-)

points.title: Potential -nga- (ndingakunceda — may I?)
points.explanation:
-nga- after the subject concord makes ability or permission: ndingakunceda? (may I help you?), ungahamba (you may go), ungafunda (you can learn). An object concord sits between -nga- and the stem, as that first form shows: ndi-nga-ku-nceda, ndi-nga-m-buza (may I ask him?).

Ukwazi (be able) takes -nga- the same way and then an infinitive: singakwazi ukunceda (we can manage to help). The negative uses -nako + infinitive: andinako ukuza (I can't come).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: 'May I help you?' asked the shopkeeper.
You can learn Xhosa in one year.
We can all manage to help.
May I ask him a question?

points.title: Stative -eka / -akala (kufuneka, iyabonakala)
points.function: Say what's visible, audible, necessary, available
points.explanation:
The stative extensions turn doing into being-done-to, with no agent named:

| verb | it means | stative | the stative means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bona | see | bonakala | be visible |
| va | hear, feel | vakala | be heard |
| funa | want | funeka | be necessary |
| fumana | get | fumaneka | be available |
| lahla | throw away | lahleka | get lost |

The ending is -eka, or the longer -akala on some stems, and a stative agrees like any other verb: intaba iyabonakala. The everyday kufuneka is funeka behind the it-subject ku-, as kuyabonakala (it is evident) is bonakala.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: The mountain is visible from afar.
drills.hint: to see flipped stative + present, class 9

drills.translation: It is necessary that we study.
drills.hint: to want flipped stative = be necessary

drills.translation: These books are available at the shop.
drills.hint: to get flipped stative + present, class 10
to throw-away flipped stative + perfect, class 7

drills.translation: It is evident that you are tired.
drills.hint: to see flipped stative + present, it-subject

points.title: Past continuous (bendifunda, ebetya)
points.explanation:
The be- auxiliary fuses with the subject concord into one prefix for an action in progress in the past:

| person | prefix | example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | bendi- | bendifunda |
| you | ubu- | ubusenza |
| he, she (class 1) | ebe- | ebetya |
| we | besi- | besimamela |
| they (class 2) | bebe- | bebedlala |

What follows the prefix is unchanged, so a stative stem stays stative: bendilele (I was asleep). The prefix also carries a question word with no verb at all — ubuphi? (where were you?).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I was reading a book yesterday.
He was eating when I arrived.
We were listening to music at night.
I was asleep when you phoned.
The mothers were shopping at the market.

points.title: Purpose: ukuze + subjunctive
points.explanation:
Ukuze opens a purpose clause and its verb goes subjunctive: the subject concord stays and the final -a becomes -e — funda kakhulu ukuze uphumelele (study hard so that you pass), sivuka kusasa ukuze sifike (we wake early so that we arrive).

A negative purpose adds -nga- after the concord and ends in -i instead of -e: ukuze kungangeni umoya (so that the wind doesn't come in).

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: Study hard so that you pass.
Study well so that you pass the exams.
We wake early so that we arrive on time.
I call you so that you help me.
Close the door so that the wind doesn't come in.
They work hard so that the children can study.

points.title: Because: kuba, ngoba — and kutheni (why)
points.explanation:
Two words open a because-clause, and one demands the reason:

- kuba — because: Andiyi esikolweni kuba ndiyagula (I am not going to school because I am ill)
- ngoba — the same job, a common variant: Ndonwabile ngoba ufikile (I am happy because you have arrived)
- kutheni — why; it opens the question and nje closes it: Kutheni le nto yenzekile nje? (why did this thing happen?)

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: I am not going to school because I am ill.
We stayed in the house because it is raining.
She is loved because she is kind.
I am happy because you have arrived.

points.title: Ideophones with ukuthi (wathi cwaka)
points.explanation:
Xhosa ideophones ride the verb -thi (say/do), and the ideophone itself never changes shape:

| ideophone | what it depicts | in a sentence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cwaka | dead silence | indlu yathi cwaka |
| gqi | a sudden appearance | wathi gqi |
| tu | saying nothing at all | wathi tu |
| saa | scattering | iinkuku zathi saa |
| qatha | popping into mind | igama lathi qatha |
| nqa | astonishment | bathi nqa |

-thi takes the subject's own concord and tense — yathi for a class 9 noun, zathi for class 10, lathi for class 5. The ideophone carries the image; -thi carries the grammar.
points.culture_note: Ideophones are performed — pitch, length, and a gesture are part of the word. Native reviewers should confirm regional forms.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: He appeared suddenly at the door.
I asked him; he said nothing at all.
The chickens scattered across the yard.
His name popped into my mind.
They were astonished when they saw the snake.

points.title: Amaqhalo — proverbs and ubuntu
points.function: Speak with the weight of the elders
points.explanation:
Amaqhalo compress the concord grammar you already know into fixed wisdom, and quoting the right one grants instant standing:

- umntu ngumntu ngabantu — a person is a person through people
- isandla sihlamba esinye — one hand washes the other
- intaka yakha ngoboya benye — a bird builds with another bird's feathers
- ubuhle bendoda ziinkomo zayo — a man's beauty is his cattle
- inyathi ibuzwa kwabaphambili — ask the ones who have gone ahead
- ukwanda kwaliwa ngumthakathi — only a witch begrudges increase

The first is the most famous sentence in the language.
points.culture_note: Ukwanda kwaliwa ngumthakathi is said to thank someone: may your generosity keep increasing — only a witch would oppose it.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: A person is a person through people.
A bird builds with another bird's feathers.
A man's beauty is his cattle.
The buffalo is asked about from those who are ahead.
Increase is begrudged only by the witch.

points.title: Hlonipha — the respect register
points.explanation:
Respect is grammatical, not only a matter of tone:

- greet an elder in the plural — molweni, even to one person
- address them as tata or mama, never by name
- treat them ngembeko (with respect)

Traditional hlonipha goes further — a makoti avoids her in-laws' names entirely, and camagu answers in ritual settings.
points.culture_note: Hlonipha is a living system, strongest in rural areas and ritual life — a native reviewer should tune these to the community the app serves.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: 'Greetings (respectful plural), father,' said the young man politely.
drills.hint: the plural greeting used to one elder

drills.translation: The bride respects (avoids) the names of her husband's parents.
We say 'father' when addressing an old man.
drills.hint: the respectful address for a man

drills.translation: When giving ritual thanks in a homestead, we say 'Camagu!'
It is not acceptable to call an elder by name.

points.title: Discourse particles (ke, nje, phofu, kaloku)
points.function: Carry the tone of a real conversation
points.explanation:
Discourse particles carry the tone of a conversation rather than its content:

- ke — then, so: masihambe ke
- nje — just, softening what you ask for: ndicela amanzi nje
- phofu — mind you, adding an aside
- kaloku — you see, after all, appealing to shared sense
- andithi — isn't it?, tagging for agreement
- mhlawumbi — perhaps, hedging

Ke and nje follow the word they colour, while phofu, kaloku and mhlawumbi open the clause.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: Mind you, he knows nothing about this.
You see, we are all still learning.

points.title: Greetings in full (molo, hamba kakuhle)
points.function: Open and close encounters like a local
points.explanation:
Molo greets one person, molweni several — and one elder, which is the respect plural. The exchange is short: Molo, unjani? — Ndiphilile, enkosi (Hello, how are you? — I am well, thank you).

Partings split by who moves: hamba kakuhle (go well) to the one leaving, sala kakuhle (stay well) to the one staying. Uxolo excuses, enkosi kakhulu thanks warmly.

references.title: Live Lingua — Peace Corps Xhosa course

drills.translation: 'How are you?' 'I am well, thank you.'

drills.hint: the farewell to the one LEAVING
the farewell to the one STAYING

drills.translation: Thank you very much for your help.
